How DAPSA is calculated

DAPSA = 68-joint tender count + 66-joint swollen count + Patient Global (0–10) + Patient Pain (0–10) + CRP (mg/dL).

cDAPSA omits CRP. Disease states: DAPSA remission ≤4, low >4–14, moderate >14–28, high >28. cDAPSA uses ≤4, >4–13, >13–27, >27.

DAPSA primarily reflects peripheral articular disease and does not capture all PsA domains such as skin disease, enthesitis, axial disease or dactylitis.

Spinal alignment / scoliosis

Use only after inspecting spinal alignment.
Convex = Bulge
How to assess and describe scoliosis

Mnemonic: Convex = Bulge. Looking at the patient from behind, select the side the spinal curve bulges toward. Right-convex means the bulge is toward the patient’s right; left-convex means it is toward the patient’s left. Avoid using the shape of the letter C as a mnemonic because it can be visually confusing.

For Adam’s forward bend test, ask the patient to bend forward with knees straight and arms relaxed, then inspect from behind for asymmetric rib or lumbar prominence. Record what you observe; a positive screening test does not by itself establish the cause or radiographic severity of scoliosis.

Cervical spine examination
Range of motion
Exact cervical rotation entered for BASMI is reused automatically.
Radicular provocative tests
Use after performing the listed tests. If abnormal, record only the positive side/pattern below.
Technique & interpretation

Spurling: gentle extension/lateral flexion toward the symptomatic side with axial compression; positive when the patient’s familiar radicular arm symptoms are reproduced.

Upper-limb tension test: progressively tension the median-nerve-biased upper limb; reproduction/asymmetry of familiar neural symptoms is positive. A negative test is particularly useful when considering cervical radiculopathy.

Cervical distraction: gentle axial traction; relief of the patient’s radicular symptoms is a positive finding.

Shoulder-abduction relief: placing the symptomatic hand on the head that relieves radicular symptoms is a positive finding. These maneuvers support clinical localization but do not independently establish a diagnosis.

Upper-limb neurologic screen
Normal shortcut = motor, C5–T1 sensory screen and biceps/brachioradialis/triceps reflexes documented as normal. Add exceptions only when abnormal.
Add abnormal upper-limb neurologic finding
Myelopathy / upper motor neuron screen
A normal screening examination does not exclude cervical myelopathy. Document abnormal signs explicitly.
Add abnormal myelopathic sign
Why screen for myelopathy?
Upper motor neuron findings such as Hoffmann sign, Babinski response, clonus, hyperreflexia and gait disturbance can support concern for cervical cord dysfunction. Individual signs are imperfect and some are relatively insensitive; interpret the pattern with the history and full neurologic examination rather than using any single sign diagnostically.

How BASMI10 is calculated
Each of the five mobility measures is converted to a 0–10 component score using the BASMI10 table. Bilateral cervical rotation, tragus-to-wall, and lumbar lateral flexion are averaged first. The five component scores are then averaged. A higher BASMI10 represents greater limitation of spinal mobility. The app does not invent mild/moderate/severe categories.

1. Perform Beighton examination

Beighton: not started

Select only the positive maneuvers as you examine them, then use Exam complete — mark remaining negative. Unselected maneuvers are never silently assumed negative.

5th finger passive dorsiflexion >90°
TechniqueWith the forearm and palm supported, passively extend the fifth MCP. Score one point on each side if it exceeds 90°.
Thumb apposition to forearm
TechniquePassively flex the thumb across the palm and toward the volar forearm. Score one point on each side when the thumb contacts the forearm.
Elbow hyperextension >10°
TechniqueWith the arm extended, assess hyperextension beyond 10°. Score each side separately.
Knee hyperextension >10°
TechniqueAssess standing or supine knee extension. Score each knee separately if hyperextension exceeds 10°.
Palms flat on floor with knees straight
TechniqueAsk the patient to bend forward with knees fully extended and place both palms flat on the floor. This contributes one point.
Use only after all Beighton maneuvers have actually been assessed.
Beighton score
0/9
Complete the examination for interpretation.
How to interpret the Beighton score
The Beighton score is a screening measure of generalized joint hypermobility, not a diagnosis of hEDS or HSD. For this adult MSK tool, the screening threshold is ≥5/9 for biologically mature/adult patients through age 50 and ≥4/9 for adults over 50. A pediatric prepubertal reference threshold of ≥6/9 is shown for education only; this app is not intended for pediatric clinical assessment.

The Beighton score is interpreted in clinical context and does not diagnose a connective-tissue disorder.

1. Focused myositis / myopathy strength examination

Strength: not started

Clinic-first workflow: document the focused examination as normal after actually testing it, then change only abnormalities. MRC grades are recorded as categorical bedside findings; 4−/4/4+ are not converted into invented numerical values.

Sets the core tested muscle groups to MRC 5/5 (single axial grade for neck flexion; bilateral grades for limb muscles) and documents normal basic function. Use only after examination.
Strength view:

Muscle power — MRC 0–5 grading

Learn MRC grading: Gravity first, then resistance

Memory ladder: 0 Nothing · 1 Flicker · 2 Slide · 3 Lift · 4 Resist · 5 Full. Start at grade 3, the gravity gate. If the limb moves through the available range against gravity, test resistance; otherwise support the limb and eliminate gravity.

0 NothingNo detectable contraction
1 FlickerPalpable or visible contraction, no movement
2 SlideActive movement with gravity eliminated
3 LiftActive movement against gravity
4 ResistAgainst gravity and resistance, weaker than expected
5 FullNormal expected power against resistance

Bedside sequence: P-S-A-R. Position, Stabilize, Ask for active movement, Resist gradually in the opposite direction. Compare sides, avoid substitutions and record pain, restricted range or poor effort. Use NA if a reliable grade cannot be assigned.

Practice retrieval: A patient can lift the leg against gravity but cannot tolerate added resistance. What grade?

Reveal answerGrade 3 if full available antigravity movement is demonstrated and the limitation is weakness, not pain or poor effort.

Muscle-specific positioning cues are shown in the table. The ladder is a teaching aid, not a replacement for supervised examination.

Select right and left limb grades independently by default. Turn on Mirror mode only when you want the same limb grade applied to the opposite side. Neck flexion uses one axial score and is never mirrored. The standardized MRC Sum Score uses six bilateral movements; additional myositis muscles are documented separately.

MRC grading & examination technique
MRC 0–5 bedside grading
  1. 5: movement against gravity plus full expected resistance.
  2. 4: movement against gravity plus some resistance, but weaker than normal.
  3. 3: movement through the available range against gravity but no added resistance.
  4. 2: movement with gravity eliminated.
  5. 1: visible or palpable contraction without joint movement.
  6. 0: no contraction.

Technique: compare both sides; position and stabilize consistently; demonstrate the movement; first establish whether the patient can move against gravity; then apply resistance gradually opposite the tested movement. Repeat if comprehension or effort is uncertain. Record pain/ROM/effort limitation rather than mislabeling it as true weakness.

The app permits 4− and 4+ as common clinical descriptors, but treats them as categorical documentation only. They are not mathematically converted.

RheumGuide MSK Examination v6.6 · Client-side examination and documentation aid. Peripheral, PsA/DAPSA, axial, hypermobility, and myositis/myopathy modules remain independently documented; combined EMR output includes only modules containing entered data.

Clinical use and safety: For qualified healthcare professionals assessing adults. This is a documentation, education and calculation aid, not a diagnostic system, permanent medical record or substitute for clinical judgment, examination or investigations. Scores measure specific domains and do not establish or exclude inflammatory disease, serious pathology, or a diagnosis. Do not base treatment decisions solely on generated scores. Verify joint localization, laterality, assessment completeness, laboratory values and units, scores and every exported report before clinical use. Software defects, transcription errors and browser or EMR incompatibilities remain possible. Do not enter identifiable information. Calculations are local; clipboard and downloaded files may persist and must be handled under applicable institutional privacy policies. Local processing does not establish regulatory compliance. How to use the joint-count tool

  1. Confirm the encounter date. Add a patient identifier and DOB only when appropriate. Age is calculated on the encounter date.
  2. Select a finding tool. The selected button stays active while you mark several joints. You can also hover or keyboard-focus any tool button for a short explanation.
  3. Mark the joint accurately. Move the pointer onto the intended joint; the blue focus halo and joint name preview show exactly which joint will be selected. Click/tap once to add the active finding; repeat with the same finding tool to remove it. For closely spaced MCP/PIP/DIP/MTP joints, the app selects the anatomically nearest joint to the pointer rather than relying on overlapping click circles.
  4. Correct mistakes immediately. Use Undo, Redo, Erase joint, or the clearing controls. Hover/focus a joint to see its current findings and whether it contributes to CDAI/DAS28.
  5. Enter PGA and PhGA. Drag either slider or type a value from 0 to 10. DAS28-CRP additionally requires CRP in mg/L.
  6. Review the 28-joint score set. Shoulders, elbows, wrists, MCPs, thumb IP/PIPs, and knees contribute to TJC/SJC. Sternoclavicular joints, hips, ankles, MTPs, and DIPs are available for additional documentation and never alter CDAI/DAS28.
  7. Complete the examination deliberately. After examining all remaining score joints and finding them normal, use the green “Mark remaining 28 normal” button, then confirm examination completion. It never overwrites joints that already have findings.
  8. Correct mistakes safely. Undo/Redo reverses recent joint changes. “Clear all joint findings” removes all joint markings and joint-specific comments. “Reset assessment” starts a completely new assessment and clears patient fields, global assessments, CRP, comments, completion status and all joint findings after confirmation.
  9. Copy or export. Copy the clinical summary or the diagram. The copied/downloaded diagram includes a legend, joint counts, and the available CDAI/DAS28-CRP scores.
Keyboard shortcuts
C — copy diagram + legend to the clipboard for pasting into an EMR, Word, PowerPoint, or another compatible app.
Q — copy the clinical summary.   P — download the diagram + legend PNG.
These single-key shortcuts work only when you are not typing in an input or comments field. The previous Alt/Option + Shift shortcuts are retained as secondary fallbacks, but some browsers or embedded pages may intercept them.
When your cursor is not inside a text/number/date field: T Tender, S Swollen, B Tender + swollen, H Thickened, D Damaged, N Not assessable, E Erase, M Mark remaining 28 normal, ? How to use.
Ctrl/Cmd + Z and Ctrl/Cmd + Y perform joint Undo/Redo when you are not editing a field. Native text-field undo is preserved while typing.
What each finding button means
Tender: Pain/tenderness elicited on joint examination. Counts toward TJC only for joints in the 28-joint score set.
Swollen: Definite palpable clinical synovial swelling. Counts toward SJC only for joints in the 28-joint score set.
Tender + swollen: Applies both active findings in one click; for a score joint it contributes to both TJC and SJC.
Thickened: Documents chronic palpable thickening without automatically calling the joint actively swollen. It does not itself increase CDAI/DAS28.
Damaged: Documents established structural damage/deformity. Damage is an overlay and can coexist with compatible active findings; it does not itself increase CDAI/DAS28.
Traditional symbols: Tender = X; Swollen = solid fill; Tender + swollen = solid fill with a contrasting X; Thickened = double ring; Damaged = diagonal slash.
Not assessable: Available in Advanced Findings for the uncommon situation where a joint genuinely cannot be examined reliably. This is distinct from an examined normal joint.
Joint note: Select this under Advanced Findings, then click any joint to add quick findings, joint-specific ROM, joint-specific special tests, limited POCUS findings, or free text. A blue speech-bubble marker shows that additional joint documentation exists. Joint notes appear in the EMR-ready summary and do not alter activity scores.
Erase joint: Clears all findings from the selected joint while leaving the rest of the examination unchanged.
Special rule for hips: Hip joints are included for documentation only. Because a routine bedside hip examination cannot reliably designate superficial swelling or synovial thickening, hips can be marked only Tender, Damaged, or Not assessable. Hip findings never contribute to CDAI or DAS28.
Precision tip: Before clicking closely spaced finger or toe joints, confirm the blue hover halo/joint label is on the intended joint. On touch devices, tap the center of the visible marker. Undo is always available if a selection is incorrect.
Safety rule: “Damaged” and “Thickened” document structural or chronic findings. They do not count as active swelling unless a compatible joint is also marked Swollen. Sternoclavicular joints, hips, ankles, MTPs, and DIPs are available for documentation but do not contribute directly to CDAI/DAS28.
